# Gospel of Thomas, Saying 64 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Source:** Nag Hammadi Codex II, p. 47-48 | Coptic

---

## Saying 64

Jesus said: "A man had guests, and when he had prepared the dinner, he sent his servant to invite the guests. He went to the first one and said to him: 'My master invites you.' He said: 'I have money with some merchants. They are coming to me this evening. I must go and give them my orders. I ask to be excused from the dinner.' He went to another and said to him: 'My master has invited you.' He said: 'I have bought a house and am required there for a day. I will have no time.' He went to another and said to him: 'My master invites you.' He said: 'A friend of mine is to be married, and I am to arrange the dinner. I shall not be able to come. I ask to be excused from the dinner.' He went to another and said to him: 'My master invites you.' He said: 'I have bought a farm. I am going to collect the rent. I shall not be able to come. I ask to be excused.' The servant came back and said to his master: 'Those whom you invited to the dinner have asked to be excused.' The master said to his servant: 'Go outside to the streets and bring back those whom you happen to meet, so that they may dine.' Businessmen and merchants will not enter the places of my Father."

---

**Council Notes:**

- Thomas's version of the Great Banquet parable (cf. Luke 14, Matt 22) has four excused guests, all with commercial or social motives. There is no violence, no burning of cities.
- The final condemnatory line is unique to Thomas: commercial preoccupation disqualifies entry into the Father's domain.
- "Places of my Father" (*topos*): LOGOS/EMET preserve "places"; PNEUMA's "domain" is interpretively richer but moves away from the Coptic *topos*.
- "Businessmen and merchants" (EMET): the two words in Coptic are *mpōle* and *emporos* — traders and merchants, which is what LOGOS also renders. Both terms preserved.
